entries.answer: Node.js is a runtime that lets JavaScript run outside the browser, on a server or a command line, and that shift is the whole reason JavaScript became a language for backend work. It is built on V8, the same JavaScript engine Chrome uses, wrapped in a standard library that includes an event loop, file system access and networking. Because the runtime is single-threaded with asynchronous input and output, it handles many concurrent connections without a thread per request, which is excellent for I/O bound work such as databases and APIs and a poor fit for CPU heavy work such as image processing. The package ecosystem on the npm registry is the largest of any language, and the common directory of missing-lockfile and left-pad incidents from 2016 are still the standard warning about depending on it.

patterns: how does the event loop work
what is the event loop in node
entries.answer: The event loop is the scheduling mechanism inside Node.js that decides what runs next, and understanding it explains almost every surprise people hit with asynchronous code. There is a call stack for synchronous work, a heap for objects, and a queue of callbacks waiting to be run. When the stack is empty the loop takes the next callback, runs it to completion, and only then looks at the queue again, which is why a long synchronous block freezes everything including the event loop itself. Non-blocking operations such as reading a file or making a request register a callback and return immediately, so thousands of them can be in flight while the process uses one thread. The consequence worth remembering is that code after an await or inside a callback always runs on a later tick than code that looks sequential, and a for loop with await inside runs the body in series unless you use Promise.all.

entries.answer: npm is the package manager that ships with Node.js and it is the default way to install dependencies and publish your own code. A project declares what it needs in package.json, and npm install reads that file, downloads the packages and their transitive dependencies into a node_modules directory, then records exact versions in a lockfile. The lockfile is the part that matters most in practice: without a committed package-lock.json, two developers on the same project can end up with different versions of a transitive dependency and a bug that reproduces on one machine only. Running a script from package.json is also the standard way to wire up a dev server or a test runner, so the commands a project uses are declared in the repository rather than living in a wiki. The two commands people need first are npm install to get everything and npm start to run the declared entry point.

entries.answer: Express is a minimal web framework for Node.js that sits on top of the built-in http module and removes the repetitive work of handling a request. Its core idea is a middleware chain: you register functions in order, each one receives the request, the response and a next callback, and each one either sends a response or passes control along, so authentication, logging, body parsing and routing become small composable pieces rather than one large handler. Routing is declarative, so you can attach handlers to a method and a path, and a request that matches no route falls through to a handler you defined for that case. It is deliberately small and leaves decisions such as templating, file uploads and database access to other packages, which is why it has stayed the most common starting point despite many newer competitors. The cost is that the same flexibility means security choices are entirely yours, and things like body size limits and header configuration have to be set deliberately.

entries.answer: Representational State Transfer is the architectural style that describes a web interface built around resources that have identities, can be represented, and respond to a small fixed set of methods. The resources are nouns in a URL, a user is at a path rather than behind a get_user action, and the HTTP method carries the meaning: GET reads and must not change anything, POST creates, PUT replaces a resource entirely, PATCH updates part of it, and DELETE removes. Responses carry status codes as part of the contract, with 200 for success, 201 for something created, 400 for a malformed request, 401 for missing authentication, 404 for a resource that does not exist and 500 for a fault on the server. The style is stateless between requests, meaning each request carries everything needed to interpret it, which is what lets any server in a pool answer any of them. The name is a description of constraints rather than a protocol, so two APIs called REST can behave very differently.
